title: Israel Yehuda and the sound of Hasidic music in David-Horodok
summary: As a composer influenced by Polish and Galician Hasidism, Yehuda offers a way to explore the community’s musical and religious culture.
editorialContent:
![David-Horodok, home of Israel Yehuda’s music](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg/1920px-%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A singer who became a composer

In the memorial book’s portrait, [Rabbi Israel Yehuda Kula](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_7bb74609d8018f28090114c8) arrives in David-Horodok not first as a composer, but as a man whose voice gathered listeners. A Galician Hasid and scholar, he served the town for six years as a *shochet*, a ritual slaughterer. The book says he came in 1926, at the prompting of his rebbe, Rabbi Moshe Perlov of Stolin. He had left Bielic in western Galicia—hence the community’s name for him, “the Galician shochet”—and lodged with Boaz Schuster on Olshaner Street.

The same account describes a town divided over the appointment of its new ritual slaughterer. Some residents questioned whether Yehuda would be too strict; others, the writer suggests, may have feared competition. But his singing made an impression across those divisions. At Passover, when he led the Prayer for Dew in the Stolin Hasidic synagogue, worshippers left other synagogues in the Shulhof courtyard to listen. The elderly Rabbi Dovidl came too. The memorial book presents this episode as both a musical triumph and a flashpoint in a local dispute: his voice drew admiration, but that attention intensified opposition.

Yehuda composed many melodies without being able to read musical notation, the book says. It portrays composition as an inward, devotional practice: he poured feeling, longing, pain and joy into tunes that listeners experienced almost as prayer. That is the memorialist’s interpretation, shaped by reverence for a murdered community figure. It does not give us scores or recordings with which to assess the music independently. Still, its description is unusually specific about how the melodies were remembered: quiet and gentle at first, then growing more ardent until they reached a fervent high point.

## The Hasidic worlds in his melodies

The memorial book locates Yehuda’s musical inheritance in Polish and Galician Hasidism, especially the tradition of [Stolin-Karlin Hasidism](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_0474901a5099684cf69dee72). It describes that influence through qualities rather than technical musical terms: warmth, enthusiasm, inner feeling and movement. Yehuda’s music, in this account, was not ornament added to religious life. Song carried meaning, and the melodies’ emotional rises and falls gave shape to yearning, joy and supplication.

That understanding appears in the particular songs the book names. Yehuda composed for the High Holy Days, including tunes for *Vayeetayu* and *Hayom Harat Olam*, and for the Sabbath, including *Menucha Vesimcha* and *Ka Echsof*. The memorialist recalls him explaining that Hasidic songs had “levels,” each suited to the feeling and spiritual quality of its words. The example of *Ka Echsof*, a Sabbath hymn of longing, makes the point: music was a way to inhabit the prayer, not merely to perform it.

The book also describes a wider communal life around song. Yehuda’s compositions were made for holidays and occasions throughout the year, for hymns and Hasidic dances, and were sung among Karlin-Stolin Hasidim beyond David-Horodok. This matters because the story is not simply that one gifted man wrote melodies. It is that his work moved through a religious network, carried by worshippers who learned and sang it together. The [Stolyn-Karlin Hasidic community](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_624401b99e04be005092c5bc) became the living setting in which the memorial book says his compositions endured.

## A meeting in Warsaw, and a journey through Russia

The book traces Yehuda’s devotion to his rebbe across a much wider geography. In 1920, it says, he met Rabbi Israelke of Stolin in Warsaw, after the two had been apart for years. The rabbi listened to Yehuda sing and praised his skill, then asked him to send special melodies for the High Holy Days. The memorial account links that separation to Yehuda’s flight from [Russia](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_cff1e16879a6b12d0e8576a8) after he was drafted into the [Russian Army](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_acfc0d0c3bfec29ee10a7757) during the [Russo-Japanese War](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_879635caaac5bf61843f6592). The two details are part of the book’s account; the records provided here do not independently document Yehuda’s military service or escape.

The memorial book gives the meeting a practical consequence: Yehuda sent melodies to the rebbe and, after Rabbi Israelke died the following year, continued composing for the High Holy Days. It says the tunes were sung in Stolin and that his Sabbath melodies entered the Karlin-Stolin repertoire. This account suggests how a local musician could belong at once to David-Horodok and to a broader Hasidic world—through a rebbe’s authority, travel, correspondence and communal singing.

The surviving evidence leaves important questions open. The memorialist says Yehuda could not read musical notes, but also says he sent the rebbe “the notes” to his songs. Were these melodies written down by someone else, transmitted in another form, or is the translation using “notes” loosely? The book does not explain. The history of [Bielic] and the possibility of locating any surviving manuscripts, recordings or later song collections would help clarify how the melodies travelled and changed.

## The family and the silence after 1942

The memorial book names Yehuda’s wife, [Bila Haya](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ed94cfff0d2dddb0b2d137ac), and their daughter, [Hana](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_985843e116ab18f2b8160934). It says that all three were murdered by the Nazis in [Kobryn](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_9c5127de0a5843ed63969501). Its date is the fourth of Cheshvan 5703. Yad Vashem’s independent entry on Kobryn provides the town’s wartime setting: German forces occupied it in June 1941, confined Jews in a ghetto, and murdered thousands in successive actions. The entry dates the liquidation of the final ghetto section to 14 October 1942. The memorial book’s date and Yad Vashem’s date are not identical; without more evidence, they should not be collapsed into a single precise date for the family’s death. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav161.html))

The larger history also places Kobryn within the German occupation of Soviet Belarus, where ghettos and mass killings formed part of the persecution and destruction of Jewish communities. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes how, after Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, German authorities established ghettos across occupied Belarus and other eastern territories, often alongside massacres. That regional context helps explain the scale of danger, but it does not independently identify Yehuda or his family. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/ghettos?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book says Yehuda’s melodies continued to be sung among Karlin-Stolin Hasidim on Sabbaths and festivals. That is a testimony to cultural survival, not proof that every composition can now be identified or attributed with certainty. The same book that preserves his name and musical legacy also marks its rupture: with the Holocaust, it says, the voices that carried the melodies were silenced. What remains is a portrait of music rooted in a particular community—shaped by Hasidic devotion, heard across synagogue boundaries, and remembered after the people who made it had been murdered.
